narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three pieces of information about you drove this outcome, ranked by importance. First, your undergraduate GPA of 3.30 was the strongest factor. Although it sits slightly above the average of accepted students (3.23), the model determined that this level of performance still increased the likelihood you would struggle with the bar exam. Second, your strong performance in your third year of law school—placing in the top decile—worked in your favor and pushed the prediction toward passing. However, this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the other factors. Third, your LSAT score of 40, which is higher than the 37.18 average among accepted students, also nudged the prediction slightly toward failure in the model’s eyes.

In short, while your recent academic record and test score are solid, the combination of these elements led the system to conclude you were more likely than not to fail the bar on the first try.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas the model flagged. Consider targeted bar-prep courses, especially those that build on undergraduate-level reasoning, and retake the LSAT if possible to raise your score further. With improved preparation, your next application or bar attempt will have a much better chance of success. (248 words)
